source.title: LawBench: Benchmarking Legal Knowledge of Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhi-Wei Fei; Xiaoyu Shen; D. Zhu; Fengzhe Zhou; Zhuo Han; Songyang Zhang; Kai Chen; Zong-Wen Shen; Ji-Dong Ge

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, a different measure from the original pretraining-loss scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are overall LawBench scores across model-size series and the authors' stated size trends. Other benchmark scores, fine-tuning comparisons, and task-by-task results are not rows because they do not test the claim versions about scaling predictability.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates off-the-shelf model families at several sizes on a new downstream setting, Chinese legal tasks. Its analysis section explicitly asks whether 'larger models perform better' holds in the legal domain, citing Kaplan et al. This bears on V6. It fits no curve, does not use pretraining loss, and its size points are not controlled for tokens or data.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say scaling up typically improves one-shot performance and lowers abstention. ChatLaw is an outlier, larger yet worse. Zero-shot results are mixed, so size alone may not improve performance.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream legal benchmark comparison across model sizes, not a held-out pretraining-loss scaling experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The size-performance pattern differs between zero-shot and one-shot settings; the authors say the improvement is more consistent in one-shot. ChatLaw is an outlier.

fits_no_version.finding: Abstention rate (failure to give an extractable answer) falls with model size, especially one-shot (Figure 4). Authors read this as better instruction following.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models abstain less or follow answer-format instructions better on domain benchmarks.

record.problems: The tested measure is an aggregate downstream benchmark score, not pretraining loss. The authors report no uncertainty estimates for the size comparisons and describe the zero-shot trend as mixed; the results do not establish predictive power or a power-law fit.
record.rows_left_out: Other model scores and task-specific benchmark results in Tables 24-31 were left out because they do not add separate model-size comparisons to the size-series results captured here.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream scores from pretraining loss; any fitted or extrapolated scaling curve. Only 2–4 uncontrolled size points per family are compared.

missing.what: Abstention rate versus model size for the same size series. Authors use it to interpret the score trends; no row records it.

record.verdict_notes: Size comparisons use independently released checkpoints, not controlled scaling runs. Token counts, data and fine-tuning differ across sizes (e.g., LLaMA 30B/65B trained on more tokens; ChatLaw sizes use different bases). There are no uncertainty estimates, and scores are confounded by answer extraction and abstention. Smallest-size rows (r1, r5, r9, r12, r15, r18, r21, r24, r27, r29, r31, r33, r35, r37) are baselines only.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' pretraining loss from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares aggregate downstream benchmark scores with model size, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a predictive scaling curve.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices.

relationships.condition: One-shot setting: LLaMA-2-Chat, Vicuna-v1.3, Baichuan, LLaMA-2-Chinese, and LLaMA-2 13B→70B
relationships.reason: Overall LawBench score rises with size in these one-shot series (r14, r19, r20, r25, r26, r30, r34).
relationships.display_finding: Overall LawBench scores increased with model size in every specified one-shot series.

relationships.condition: Non-monotonic or flat steps: zero-shot LLaMA-2 and Vicuna; one-shot LLaMA 13B→30B and LLaMA-2 7B→13B; zero-shot LLaMA-2-Chat 13B→70B
relationships.reason: Gains are absent or reverse at some steps even within rising families. Authors say improvement is more consistent one-shot than zero-shot (r7, r10, r11, r13, r17, r22, r23).
relationships.display_finding: Some size increases produced no gain or reduced performance even within generally improving families, with one-shot gains more consistent than zero-shot gains.

relationships.reason: Overall zero-shot score does not improve across a ~9x size range, falling from 9.72 to 8.44 (r2, r3, r4).
relationships.display_finding: The overall zero-shot score fell from 9.72 to 8.44 across an approximately ninefold increase in LLaMA size.

relationships.condition: ChatLaw 13B vs 33B, zero- and one-shot (different base models)
relationships.reason: The larger model scores lower in both settings: 32.76→26.14 and 32.63→25.41. Authors call it an outlier, and the base models differ (r36, r38).
relationships.display_finding: ChatLaw scores fell from 32.76 to 26.14 zero-shot and from 32.63 to 25.41 one-shot, although the base models differed and the authors described the result as an outlier.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: One-shot LLaMA-2, LLaMA-2-Chat, Baichuan, and LLaMA-2-Chinese size comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Scores rise across the reported sizes in these series, though this is not evidence of a fitted predictive scaling curve (r12-r14, r18-r20, r29-r30, r33-r34).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Zero-shot size comparisons and the LLaMA and Vicuna series
reader_labels.reason: The authors report mixed zero-shot size results; the tabulated LLaMA and Vicuna scores also move up and down rather than improving monotonically (r1-r4, r21-r23).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: ChatLaw-13B versus ChatLaw-33B, in zero-shot and one-shot settings
reader_labels.reason: The larger ChatLaw checkpoint has a lower overall score in both settings, matching the authors' stated outlier observation (r35-r38).
